loc: Lesson05_Restores_and_Day_to_Day_Administration.html · Access control section, "The four roles you will reach for" table, k10-basic row
orig: Operational access in specific namespaces. Within assigned namespaces the holder may manually back up and restore applications, create and modify policies, view application, action and restore point details, and cancel actions [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.272].
prop: Operational access in specific namespaces. Within assigned namespaces the holder may manually back up and restore applications, create and modify policies, view application, action and restore point details, and cancel actions [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.272]. [VERIFY: does this role also permit deleting a restore point or a policy, or is deletion reserved to k10-admin? State it explicitly — "who can delete these backups" is the first question most CISOs ask, and this table is where a director would look for the answer.]
why: The RBAC table names every other capability for k10-basic (backup, restore, create/modify policies, view, cancel) but is silent on delete. A director cannot answer the classic 'who can delete backups' question from this material for the one role most of the team will actually hold. Per the hard rules, a missing accountability answer must be flagged as a question, not filled in from assumption — this is exactly that case.

orig: The same information appears in tabular form under the graph, beginning with a summary of total actions, average action duration, the number of data artifacts and their size, followed by recent actions including the policy that generated each one, the number of child actions, the number of applications included in the run, and start and completion times [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.311].
prop: The same information appears in tabular form under the graph, beginning with a summary of total actions, average action duration, the number of data artifacts and their size, followed by recent actions including the policy that generated each one, the number of child actions, the number of applications included in the run, and start and completion times [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.311]. [VERIFY: does this activity view, or any audit log, record which authenticated user triggered a manual backup, restore, or deletion? Name the screen here — a director will be asked this before almost anything else, and the course currently answers 'what happened' without ever answering 'who did it.']
why: Every layer of monitoring described in Modules 04 and 05 (dashboard states, Prometheus action metrics, the activity table) reports on actions, policies, and outcomes but never on the identity of the user who triggered a manual action. Audit trail is named explicitly in this persona's scope as a director-owned concern; the course teaches 'what happened' monitoring thoroughly and is silent on 'who did it' accountability, which is the harder and more important half for an audit conversation.

prop: Read that guidance as a job description change. Under it, application teams create and manage their own backup policies, set schedules, and determine retention settings [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1092], and your role moves from operating every job to designing the guardrails those teams work inside. Decide, before you delegate, whether your team still owns reporting the aggregate compliance number to leadership once application teams own their own policies — this module does not say, and it is the first thing to settle before self-service rolls out. The routine in the next section is what that role looks like day to day.
why: The course correctly frames multi-tenancy/self-service as a real operating-model shift for the backup team, but never addresses who is accountable for rolling up compliance status once policy ownership decentralizes to application teams — which is precisely the kind of ownership question a director must settle before staffing a rollout, not discover afterward.

loc: Lesson05_Restores_and_Day_to_Day_Administration.html · Section 01 — "Building a policy: schedule, snapshot, export, retention"
orig: A new policy can be created from the Policies page or from the Applications page, and starting from the Applications page pre-populates the policy name and the namespace selection [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.347].
prop: Add a stage-by-stage interactive or screenshot sequence for creating a policy end to end — selection, snapshot frequency, export toggle and location profile, retention, save — matching the treatment Module 03 gives the Helm install (its "click each stage" flow with what-you-should-see at every step).
why: Building and scheduling a policy is this course's stated week-one task, and every other hands-on procedure in the course (the Helm install, the storage annotation, the RBAC assignment) gets a concrete click sequence or command. This section gives me the concepts and a settings table but never a rehearsed path through the actual New Policy dialog, so I have the vocabulary without having actually walked the form once.

loc: Lesson05_Restores_and_Day_to_Day_Administration.html · Section 04 — "The four roles you will reach for"
orig: that Role needs a RoleBinding in the release namespace, and Veeam Kasten creates one for the default group k10:admins, so adding the user to that group covers both bindings at once [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.268].
prop: Connect this sentence to an actual action: is "adding the user to k10:admins" done through the RBAC dashboard form shown later in this section (using Group as the subject type), asserted by the identity provider/OIDC token, or something else? Show it as a fourth screenshot alongside the three Add Assignment examples already in the section, or state explicitly which of those it is.
why: The module never closes the loop between this instruction and an executable step. Kubernetes has no built-in "add user to group" primitive outside a binding or an identity provider claim, so as written I don't know whether to create another ClusterRoleBinding by hand, use the dashboard's Group subject field, or configure something upstream in my auth provider.
